Rejected — importing a term he uses ELSEWHERE into a claim where he did not use it is exactly the outside-knowledge-injected-as-Wallach defect, and modern-voice summary latitude covers units/phrasing, not a qualifier that changes scope. The fix costs nothing: his own word is shorter, broader, and correct. The edit is minimum-force (one descriptor deleted) and leaves the rest intact, and I independently confirmed the remaining elements are faithful: "Vitamins and minerals are the backbone... your 'therapeutic' food supplements" sits immediately before the quote in the span, licensing the vitamins/minerals substitution; the "better than nothing but will not" hedge is verbatim-exact; the nine-item list is complete and in source order; "etc."->"among them" is honest; "pyorrhea (gum disease)" is a correct minimal gloss. Non-blocking style note: "serious disease" (singular) + "among them" reads awkwardly; plural "serious diseases" without "degenerative" would be equally faithful and smoother — optional, not an objection.

The defect is real and source-grounded — the span twice states causation ("direct result of," "caused by") where claim_text says "worsened by" — but it errs in the CONSERVATIVE direction (understating Wallach's blame of physicians rather than overstating it), so no reader is misled toward harm and no number, dose, or unit is affected. A reviewer who treats "worsened by" as acceptable loose compression of a causal claim would reasonably leave this as-is; I flagged it because the shift changes Wallach's stance from "the doctors caused these deaths" to "the doctors made it worse," and stance fidelity is the point of the summary layer. Three of the four claim elements are clean. page_image_available is false, so the span was my only arbiter; nothing in my judgment hinged on unreadable material, and I imported no outside-world knowledge about the 1993 heat wave, heat stroke physiology, or sodium — the correction is composed entirely from wording present in the span.

ver.why: The original genuinely misrepresents the source, so the default-to-revert bar is cleared. The span carries two independent explicit causal assertions -- "a salt deficiency CAUSED BY the allopathic paranoia of salt" and "The human tragedy of the heat wave of '93 was A DIRECT RESULT OF the allopathic doctors who put their charges (their patients) on reduced or salt free diets for high blood pressure or heart disease" -- while the original claim_text renders this as "worsened by doctor-ordered low-salt diets." That is a directional downgrade from primary cause to aggravating factor, not a stylistic nuance: Wallach's argument turns on the victims BEING the low-salt-diet cohort, which he closes with the medical examiner's "the only common denominator we found in the dead and affected... was that they all had heart disease or high blood pressure" plus "as we predicted they had all been placed on low salt or no salt diets by their physicians." "Worsened by" severs that identification. The claim is tagged low-salt-critique, so the indictment is load-bearing content, not incidental color. Adversarial check of the proposed text found no over-reach: every element traces to the span -- heat-stroke deaths ("hundreds dying"/"your basic heat stroke"), deadly July 1993 US east-coast heat wave (verbatim from span), "simple salt/sodium deficiency" (exact verbatim), "easily remedied with water and salt" (supported by "any boy scout could diagnose and recognize and remedy with water and salt"), and the corrected causal clause with "for high blood pressure or heart disease" lifted straight from the span rather than supplied from outside knowledge. No injected facts, no number/unit asserted, no misattribution, nothing faithful dropped; "allopathic doctors" to "doctors" is acceptable modern voice. RESIDUAL (not grounds to block, flagged for a later pass): the doctor-causation clause lives in the source_span but not in the verbatim, which stops at "...remedy with water and salt." This was equally true of the original wording, so the edit does not worsen verbatim coverage -- it makes an already-span-only assertion accurate. A future pass could widen the verbatim to include the immediately following "yes, a salt deficiency caused by the allopathic paranoia of salt" to bring the claim_text's causal assertion under verbatim guard. No page image needed; the span is fully legible and decisive on the causal wording, so escalation is unwarranted.

"worsened by" for "exacerbated by" and "high in" for "rich in" are modern-voice glosses of equal strength; dropping "also" changes nothing. The hedge shifts position (source: a disease that "can be produced by"; claim: CF "can be" a disease produced by) but both are hedged and neither strengthens the other — faithful compression, not a qualifier-shift. No injected outside fact, no number or unit, no inversion. One observation I am flagging rather than hiding: the stored verbatim is cut short at "...low in vitamin E" and omits "and rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids", a clause claim_text does assert. That clause IS byte-present in the source span, so claim_text remains fully source-grounded, and the cut does not fall where the source contradicts (not the severed-quote signature). Per the rubric truncation alone is not a defect, and any fix would belong to the verbatim field, not claim_text — so I am not proposing a claim_text edit. adj.concern: claim_text fabricates a causal mechanism by splicing two separate source statements: it says the particles are "so small ... that they don't dissolve into individual atoms." The source's own "so small that" clause resolves to a DIFFERENT consequent — "so small that they cannot be seen with the naked eye-about one billion of these colloid particles would fit into 0.01 cubic inch." The source attributes non-separation not to smallness but to the particles "remain[ing] grouped together to form solute particles," and it explicitly states colloidal particles are "just barely LARGER than most molecules" and "too large" to pass a semi-permeable membrane. So the claim's smallness->non-dissolution link is both absent from and contrary to the source. Secondary qualifier-shifts in the same sentence group: the verbatim's hedge "a larger number if not all of the particles are within a range" is flattened to "the particles stay within" (strengthening to all particles), and "about 1 to 100 nanometers" inserts a hedge over the source's exact "(1nm to 100nm)".
adj.proposed_edit: What is a colloidal mineral - and what does 'nano-technology' have to do with it? Wallach describes a colloid as a substance existing as ultra-fine particles suspended in a medium of different matter - so small (about one billion would fit into 0.01 cubic inch) that they cannot be seen with the naked eye. In the colloidal state, he says, the particles remain grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in a true solution. He notes colloids remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble as long as a larger number of the particles, if not all, stay within the colloidal size range of 1nm to 100nm - a range, he points out, known as 'nano-technology.' In his words: "The interesting thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as 'nano-technology.'"
adj.honesty: I audited this fresh and did not go looking for a defect — the majority of the claim (the colloid definition, the one-billion/0.01-cubic-inch figure, the salt/true-solution contrast, the nano-technology attribution) is faithfully compressed from the span. What tipped this from leave-as-is to rewrite is that the source contains the exact "so small that" construction with a different consequent (cannot be seen with the naked eye), which makes the swap a demonstrable splice rather than my inference about loose phrasing. I am medium rather than high confidence because a charitable reader could parse "so small (...) that they don't dissolve" as loose apposition rather than a causal claim, and because both component facts are individually true to the source; the defect lives entirely in the connective. The verbatim quote is reproduced in claim_text with the full hedge intact, which mitigates reader harm. I imported no outside chemistry knowledge — every element of the proposed_edit is traceable to a phrase in the provided span, and the 'In his words' quote is byte-unchanged. The two secondary qualifier-shifts are minor on their own and I would not have recommended a rewrite for them alone.

ver.why: The original genuinely misrepresents the source, so the default-to-revert presumption is overcome. The span contains its own "so small that" construction with a specific consequent — "so small that they cannot be seen with the naked eye-about one billion of these colloid particles would fit into 0.01 cubic inch" — and separately attributes non-separation to grouping: molecules "do not separate into atoms as with a true solution ... but rather the colloidal particle remains grouped together to form solute particles." The original claim_text lifted the parenthetical off the first sentence, discarded its actual consequent (naked-eye invisibility, a real source fact thereby lost), and welded "so small ... that" onto the non-dissolution consequent. English "so X that Y" forces a causal reading and there is no appositive structure to escape it, so the text asserts a smallness→non-dissolution mechanism that is absent from the source AND cuts against Wallach's own framing, which stresses these particles are "just barely larger than most molecules" and "too large" to pass a semi-permeable membrane. That is clause substitution and mechanism fabrication, not compression — the defect class §00.A exists to stop. It slipped because the verbatim covers only the nano-technology sentence; the entire definition/salt half of claim_text is span-backed only and unguarded (big claim_text, small verbatim). Reviewer's hedge point is also real: "a larger number if not all of the particles" → "the particles stay within" universalizes what the source explicitly declines to universalize. Their third point ("about 1 to 100 nanometers" over exact "(1nm to 100nm)") is thin and would not alone justify a rewrite; the verdict does not rest on it. The proposed edit is a faithful correction, not an over-reach: every element traces to the span ("suspended in a medium of different matter" verbatim, naked-eye consequent restored to its own clause, grouping-vs-true-solution restored, hedge and exact range restored), it introduces nothing new, it preserves the verbatim unchanged, and its omissions ("(Angstrom unit)", "at different concentrations", "just barely larger than most molecules") are omissions rather than distortions. Resolvable from the span alone; no page image needed.

Source and the claim's OWN verbatim both read "Vanadium appears to function like insulin"; claim_text asserts it flatly as "Vanadium functions like insulin." adj.proposed_edit: Bismuth is not one of Wallach's essential nutrients, but he gives it a memorable entry. Chinese alchemists used it to treat gastric ulcers and gastroenteritis (stomach and intestinal inflammation) for more than 8,000 years, and today it is the pink liquid in over-the-counter GI remedies like Pepto-Bismol. His larger point is a myth-buster: stress has historically been blamed as the cause of gastric, peptic and duodenal ulcers, but the true cause turned out to be infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori - a link Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed in 1983 (and one already known in pigs back in 1952). His treatment of choice is a two-to-four-week course of tetracycline antibiotics, antacids and bismuth subsalicylate. In his words: "Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as Helicobacter pylori. Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D. and pathologist J. Robin Warren proposed their theory for the bacterial cause of gastric ulcers in 1983. The bacterial cause (H. pylori) for gastric ulcers was known in pigs in 1952."

CONFIRMED DEFECT 2 (weaker, but free to fix) — qualifier shift. Source hedges twice: "appears to have a lipotrophic function that may originate from"; original asserts flatly "it has a lipotrophic (fat-handling) role." adj.proposed_edit: Essential fatty acids (EFA) are the fats the body cannot make for itself and so must get from food. A shortage is especially damaging in infants.
